before.title: The boundary of a bounded smooth domain is a compact embedded hypersurface
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the boundary-chart and surface-measure interfaces cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]); no other choice principle is used. Let $k\ge1$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^k$ domain in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] (nonempty, bounded, open, and locally exactly the one-sided subgraph of a $C^k$ graph function over a hyperplane). Then:
(a) [Compactness and finiteness] $\partial D$ is nonempty and compact; the complement $\mathbb R^3\setminus\partial D$ need not be connected here. Moreover $\partial D$ has finitely many connected components, and each connected component of $\partial D$ is compact.
(b) [Finite embedded presentation] the local boundary charts give finitely many regular injective $C^k$ parametrisations of $\partial D$ with $C^k$ coordinate transitions, of the graph type required by [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]: writing a chart as $R(p)=(y,s)$, the graph map $y\mapsto R^{-1}(y,h(y))$ is injective, of class $C^k$, with $C^k$ inverse (the inverse is the restriction of the $C^\infty$ projection $R(p)\mapsto y$, composed with $R^{-1}$); consequently $\partial D$ is a compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurface, and for $k\ge1$ it carries the finite surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]].
(c) [Normal field] the outward unit normal $\nu$ of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a continuous unit normal field on $\partial D$, with $\nu(x)$ orthogonal to the tangent plane of the graph chart at each $x$; it is the field used by the Green and divergence items cited by this page's consumers.
The statement is geometric: it asserts no differentiability of $D$ beyond $C^k$, no boundedness of chart derivatives beyond the compact patches, and no connectedness of either $D$ or $\partial D$.
before.strategy: All claims are read off the local graph definition; the only points worth recording are the exact suppliers. Nonemptiness: if $\partial D$ were empty then, since $\partial D=\overline D\setminus\operatorname{int}(D)$ and $D$ is open with $\operatorname{int}(D)=D$ ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[def-metric-topology]]), $\overline D=D$, so $D$ and $\mathbb R^3\setminus D$ would be disjoint nonempty open sets covering $\mathbb R^3$, contradicting the connectedness of $\mathbb R^3$; the connectedness follows from polygonal connectedness ([[cor-rn-is-polygonally-connected-and-locally-path-connected]], [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]), and $\mathbb R^3\setminus D\ne\emptyset$ because $D$ is bounded while $\mathbb R^3$ is not, with $D\ne\emptyset$ by hypothesis. Compactness: $\partial D\subseteq\overline D$ is closed by [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]] and bounded because $D$ is bounded, so [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] applies; a closed subset of a compact space is compact by the definition of compactness ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Finitely many components: $\mathbb R^3$ is locally connected ([[cor-rn-is-polygonally-connected-and-locally-path-connected]], [[def-locally-connected]]), hence so is the subspace $\partial D$; each component of a locally connected space is open, so the components form an open cover of the compact space $\partial D$ with pairwise disjoint members, and any finite subcover already equals the whole family, giving finitely many components. Explicitly, if $C$ is a component and $x\in C$, local connectedness gives a connected open neighbourhood $V$ of $x$; $V\subseteq C$ by maximality of components, so $C=\bigcup_{x\in C}V_x$ is open; components are closed by [[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]] and [[thm-unions-of-connected-sets]], and a closed subspace of a compact space is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Presentation: at each $x\in\partial D$ the boundary chart supplies $W$, a rigid motion $R$, a ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{2}$ and $h\in C^{k}(B)$ with $R(\partial D\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s):s=h(y)\}$. The graph map $X(y):=R^{-1}(y,h(y))$ is injective and $C^{k}$ (components built from $h$ and the inverse rigid motion by the algebra and chain rules, [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); its inverse is the $C^\infty$ map $p\mapsto y(R(p))$ restricted to the graph, so $X$ is an embedding onto its image. The domains $W$ cover the compact set $\partial D$, so finitely many of them cover it, and after restricting each parametrisation to a compactly contained concentric ball — the convention of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] — the chart transitions (compositions of graph maps with rigid motions) are $C^{k}$. This is exactly the finite presentation required by [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; the surface measure is finite by its chart formula and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], because the finitely many chart domains are bounded and their Gram densities are continuous, hence bounded, on the compactly contained parameter sets. The normal claim is the definitional statement of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], whose overlap agreement is discharged there; the inner products in the orthogonality statement are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and continuity of the norm used to normalise is [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]. The choice cost is exactly the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the surface-measure interface; no other selection is made.

after.title: The boundary of a bounded smooth domain is a compact embedded hypersurface
after.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the boundary-chart and surface-measure interfaces cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]); no other choice principle is used. Let $k\ge1$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^k$ domain in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] (nonempty, bounded, open, and locally exactly the one-sided subgraph of a $C^k$ graph function over a hyperplane). Then:
(a) [Compactness and finiteness] $\partial D$ is nonempty and compact; the complement $\mathbb R^3\setminus\partial D$ need not be connected here. Moreover $\partial D$ has finitely many connected components, and each connected component of $\partial D$ is compact.
(b) [Finite embedded presentation] the local boundary charts give finitely many regular injective $C^k$ parametrisations of $\partial D$ with $C^k$ coordinate transitions, of the graph type required by [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]: writing a chart as $R(p)=(y,s)$, the graph map $y\mapsto R^{-1}(y,h(y))$ is injective, of class $C^k$, with $C^k$ inverse (the inverse is $p\mapsto\pi(R(p))$ restricted to the graph, where $\pi(y,s)=y$); consequently $\partial D$ is a compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurface, and for $k\ge1$ it carries the finite surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]].
(c) [Normal field] the outward unit normal $\nu$ of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a continuous unit normal field on $\partial D$, with $\nu(x)$ orthogonal to the tangent plane of the graph chart at each $x$; it is the field used by the Green and divergence items cited by this page's consumers.
The statement is geometric: it asserts no differentiability of $D$ beyond $C^k$, no boundedness of chart derivatives beyond the compact patches, and no connectedness of either $D$ or $\partial D$.
after.strategy: The boundary is nonempty: otherwise the nonempty open bounded $D$ would also be closed and disconnect connected $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[cor-rn-is-polygonally-connected-and-locally-path-connected]], [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]). It is closed and bounded, hence compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]. At every boundary point first shrink its graph chart to the inverse image of a small flattening cylinder $B'\times(-b,b)$ with $\overline{B'}$ compactly contained in the original parameter ball. Its boundary patch is exactly the graph $X(y)=R^{-1}(y,h(y))$ over the connected ball $B'$. The graph is homeomorphic to $B'$ by the coordinate projection, so is a connected relatively open neighbourhood in $\partial D$. Arbitrarily small such graph neighbourhoods prove local connectedness of $\partial D$ directly; local connectedness is not inherited by arbitrary Euclidean subspaces. A component is open because each of these connected neighbourhoods meeting it lies in it by maximality; it is closed because the closure of a connected set is connected (if separated, the two relative open separating sets would also separate the dense original connected set). Compactness and the open component cover therefore give finitely many components, each closed and compact. For the embedded presentation, the graph maps are injective and $C^k$, and their derivatives have independent tangent columns since projection onto $y$ has derivative the identity; their inverses are the restricted coordinate projections. Transitions are the corresponding projections composed with the graph maps and rigid motions, hence $C^k$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Choose these smaller chart neighbourhoods at every point first, and only then take a finite subcover of the compact boundary. The associated larger charts provide room for compact supports of a subordinate partition; their graph densities and derivatives are bounded on those compact supports. This supplies exactly the finite compact embedded hypersurface and finite surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. The outward graph normal is the continuous $(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ transported by the rigid coordinates; overlap agreement is supplied by [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. No domain or boundary connectedness is assumed, and the only choice assumption used is the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

before.title: The vacuum region around compact smooth conductors is a bounded smooth domain
before.strategy:
Write $K:=\overline{D_1}\cup\cdots\cup\overline{D_m}$, a compact subset of the open set $\Omega$; for $m=0$ the statements reduce to $\Omega_v=\Omega$ by convention.
(a) $\Omega_v$ is open as the intersection of the open set $\Omega$ with the complement of the closed set $K$ ([[def-metric-topology]]), bounded because $\Omega$ is, and nonempty: the distance functions $x\mapsto d(x,\overline{D_j})$ are continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]) on the nonempty compact boundary $\partial\Omega$ ([[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]], [[def-metric-compactness]]); each attains a positive minimum $\delta_j>0$ by [[thm-extreme-value-metric]] since $\partial\Omega\cap\overline{D_j}=\emptyset$, and any point of $\Omega$ within distance $\tfrac12\min_j\delta_j$ of $\partial\Omega$ (which exists because $\Omega$ is nonempty open and is approached by boundary points) lies in $\Omega_v$ ([[def-metric-ball]]).
(b) $\partial(\Omega\setminus K)=\partial\Omega\cup\partial K$ for compact $K\subset\Omega$: if $x\in\partial\Omega$ then every ball about $x$ meets $\Omega$ and $\mathbb R^3\setminus\Omega$, and balls small enough to avoid $K$ meet $\Omega\setminus K$; if $x\in\partial K$ then $x\in\Omega$ and every ball about $x$ meets both $K$ and its complement, the latter inside $\Omega$ for small balls; and no point of $\Omega$ outside $\partial K$ is a boundary point of $\Omega\setminus K$, because a point of the open set $\Omega\setminus K$ has a ball inside it, while a point of the interior of $K$ has a ball inside $K$, hence outside $\Omega\setminus K$ ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[def-metric-topology]]). Here $\partial K=\partial D_1\cup\cdots\cup\partial D_m$ since pairwise disjoint closed sets have pairwise disjoint boundaries, and $\partial\Omega\cap K=\emptyset$ because $K\subset\Omega$ with $\Omega$ open.
(c) Local graph property. At a point of $\partial\Omega$: $\operatorname{dist}(\partial\Omega,K)=:\delta>0$ by the same compactness argument as in (a), so a ball about the point disjoint from $K$ exists, and inside it $\Omega_v$ agrees with $\Omega$, whose boundary chart from the hypothesis gives the one-sided subgraph representation. At a point of $\partial D_j$: shrink the $D_j$-chart $W$ so that $W\subset\Omega$ and $W\cap\overline{D_i}=\emptyset$ for $i\ne j$ (possible by disjointness and openness), so that $\Omega_v\cap W=W\setminus(D_j\cap W)$; in the chart coordinates $(y,s)$ with $D_j\cap W=\{s<h(y)\}$ this is the supergraph $\{s>h(y)\}$, and applying the rigid reflection $(y,s)\mapsto(y,-s)$ exhibits it as the subgraph of the $C^k$ function $g=-h$ ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). These charts, together with $\partial\Omega$'s, cover $\partial\Omega_v$, so the local graph property holds with the same regularity $k$.
The normal statement of (c) is the definitional normal of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]: in the reflected chart the graph is $g=-h$, and transporting it back through the reflection multiplies the normal by $-1$; the definition's overlap agreement discharges consistency. For (d), the local graph property restricts to each connected component (any chart meeting the component lies inside it, and the component of an open set is open, [[thm-continuity-preimage-characterisation]] with the component's defining property); compactness of the individual pieces is [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]. No choice beyond the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the surface interface is used; no connectedness of $\Omega_v$ is asserted or needed.

after.title: The vacuum region around compact smooth conductors is a bounded smooth domain
after.strategy: Let $K=\bigcup_j\overline D_j$. It is compact, contained in open $\Omega$, and its constituent closures are pairwise disjoint. For $m=0$, $K=\varnothing$. Thus $\Omega_v=\Omega\setminus K$ is open and bounded. It is nonempty: choose a boundary point of nonempty bounded $\Omega$ by [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]; a small neighbourhood of that point avoids compact $K$ and contains interior points of $\Omega$. At an outer boundary point shrink the $\Omega$ graph cylinder to avoid $K$; locally the vacuum is the same subgraph as $\Omega$. At a point of $\partial D_j$ shrink the $D_j$ chart cylinder to lie inside $\Omega$ and avoid every other closed body. Precisely $\Omega_v\cap W=W\setminus\overline D_j$, not $W\setminus D_j$: in graph coordinates its inequality is strictly $s>h(y)$. Reflection $w=-s$ makes this the subgraph $w<-h(y)$ with $C^k$ graph. These local charts also show $\partial\Omega_v=\partial\Omega\sqcup\bigsqcup_j\partial D_j$, since the disjoint compact closures prevent other bodies from hiding or touching any boundary piece. The outward normal is the outer-domain normal on $\partial\Omega$, and its negative on $\partial D_j$, because the latter vacuum chart is the exterior of the body. The graph-normal formula in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] verifies this sign. All boundary pieces are compact smooth hypersurfaces by [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]. For components, every point of the open vacuum has a connected open ball inside it; hence its connected component is open. Every boundary point of a component lies on $\partial\Omega_v$: a connected ball inside $\Omega_v$ cannot meet two components. Choose a small flattened cylinder at such a boundary point whose vacuum half-cylinder is connected. Because that half-cylinder meets the component, all of it lies in the component; its graph is therefore the component's local boundary. Thus the component is a bounded $C^k$ domain with the inherited normal on the restricted boundary. A finite cover of compact $\partial\Omega_v$ by such connected one-sided graph cylinders meets only finitely many vacuum components. Every nonempty bounded open component has a boundary point, so there are only finitely many components. A boundary component of $\Omega_v$ is incident to a single vacuum component: the incident component is locally constant along each connected graph boundary patch, hence constant along that boundary component. Consequently each $\partial U$ is a union of the incident compact boundary components, not necessarily the entire displayed disjoint union. None of these conclusions asserts vacuum connectedness. The corrected separation hypothesis excludes tangent bodies: two tangent balls have disjoint open interiors but a touching point of their closures does not admit the asserted disjoint single-boundary chart.

before.title: Uniqueness for harmonic functions on a punctured half-space with zero trace, decaying at the pole and at infinity
before.strategy:
Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By (iv) choose $R>\max(2a,|p|)$ with $|w|\le\varepsilon$ on $H\setminus\overline B_R(0)$; by (iii) choose $0<\delta<\min(a,R-|p|)/2$ with $|w|\le\varepsilon$ on $H\cap B_\delta(p)$. Put
$$U:=\bigl(B_R(0)\setminus\overline B_\delta(p)\bigr)\cap H.$$
Then $U$ is a nonempty bounded open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ (an intersection of open sets, bounded by $B_R$ and nonempty because $(0,0,R/2)$ or a nearby point avoids the small ball; [[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-topology]]). By the choice of $\delta<R-|p|$, the closure $\overline U$ is contained in $\overline H\setminus\{p\}$: if $|x-p|\ge\delta$ and $x\in\overline H$ then $x\ne p$, and if $x\in\partial H$ then $w(x)=0$ is defined. Hence $w|_{\overline U}$ is continuous and $w|_U$ is $C^2$ with $\Delta w=0$. Apply the weak maximum principle ([[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]]) to $w$ on $U$: $\max_{\overline U}w=\max_{\partial U}w$. Now
$$\partial U\subseteq \partial B_R(0)\cup\partial H\cup\partial B_\delta(p),$$
and on the three pieces the values are controlled: on $\partial B_R(0)\cap\overline H$ we have $|w|\le\varepsilon$ by the choice of $R$ (note $\overline U\cap\partial B_R\subseteq H\setminus\overline B_R$ requires $|x|=R\ge R$, giving $|w|\le\varepsilon$ as soon as we chose $R$ with the inequality on $|x|\ge R$; adjust $R$ slightly upward if needed); on $\partial H\cap\overline U$ we have $w=0$; and on $\partial B_\delta(p)$ we have $|w|\le\varepsilon$. Hence $\max_{\partial U}w\le\varepsilon$ and, applying the same argument to $-w$ (also harmonic), $\min_{\partial U}w\ge-\varepsilon$; thus $|w|\le\varepsilon$ on $\overline U$. Every point $y\in H\setminus\{p\}$ lies in $U$ for the parameters chosen as follows: first fix $\varepsilon$ and $R,\delta$ as above with $R>\max(2a,|p|,|y|)$ and $\delta$ additionally smaller than $|y-p|$; then $y\in U$ and $|w(y)|\le\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $w(y)=0$; $y$ was arbitrary in $H\setminus\{p\}$. The argument uses only the continuity and $C^2$-harmonicity of $w$, the three boundary/limit conditions, and the weak maximum principle on the bounded open set $U$; it does not use connectedness of $U$ (the principle is stated for arbitrary bounded open sets), any removable-singularity theory, or any choice principle beyond those carried by the cited suppliers.

after.title: Uniqueness for harmonic functions on a punctured half-space with zero trace, decaying at the pole and at infinity
after.strategy: Fix $y\in H\setminus\{p\}$ and $\eta>0$. Choose $R>\max(2a,|y|)$ large enough that $|w|\le\eta$ on $H\cap\{|x|\ge R\}$, enlarging the decay threshold slightly; choose $0<\delta<\min(a/2,|y-p|,R-|p|)$ so small that $|w(x)|\le\eta/|x-p|$ whenever $0<|x-p|\le\delta$. On the nonempty bounded open $U=(B_R(0)\setminus\overline B_\delta(p))\cap H$, the functions $\pm w-\eta-\eta/|x-p|$ are harmonic and continuous on $\overline U$: the barrier $|x-p|^{-1}$ is harmonic off its pole by [[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]]. On the plane they are nonpositive because $w=0$; on the outer sphere they are nonpositive by decay; on the inner sphere they are nonpositive by the sub-Coulomb pole condition. The weak maximum principle [[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]] therefore gives $|w(y)|\le\eta(1+|y-p|^{-1})$. Let $\eta\downarrow0$ with $y$ fixed to obtain $w(y)=0$. This proves uniqueness for all sub-Coulomb remainders, including arbitrary bounded remainders and the earlier zero-remainder-limit class, without a removable-singularity theorem or extra boundary smoothness assumption.

before.title: Perfect conductor equilibrium model
before.statement:
Adopt as a physical model of ideal electrostatic conductors, for the classical laboratory framework of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]: a **conductor configuration** consists of the following data, and every model of this postulate is required to satisfy the clauses below. No experiment is reported and no empirical value is inferred; this is an explicitly adopted equilibrium idealization together with its geometric and source conventions.
(a) [Geometry] a laboratory region $\Omega\times I$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ open, a finite family $D_1,\dots,D_m$ ($m\ge1$) of pairwise disjoint bounded $C^\infty$ domains in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] with closures strictly inside $\Omega$ (the **conductor bodies**), the **conductor** $D:=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_m$, its **surface** $\partial D$, and the **vacuum region** $\Omega_v:=\Omega\setminus\overline D$. By [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]] and [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]], $\partial D=\partial D_1\cup\cdots\cup\partial D_m$ is a disjoint union of compact embedded $C^\infty$ hypersurfaces and $\Omega_v$ is again a bounded $C^\infty$ domain, whose boundary charts restrict the charts of $\Omega$ and $D_j$ as there recorded; we additionally require $\Omega_v$ to be connected (configurations whose vacuum region is separated by the conductors, for instance by an enclosing closed shell, are outside this model as formulated here).
(b) [Equilibrium and sources] the configuration is in the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] on the vacuum region: $B=0$, $J=0$, $E$ is the fixed-time electric field of [[def-em-fields]], the volume source density $\rho_v$ is a continuous real map on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ (C m$^{-3}$, [[def-em-sources]]) extended by zero to $D$; the **conductor charge is a stationary surface charge**, i.e. a continuous density $\sigma:\partial D\to\mathbb R$ (C m$^{-2}$) whose pairing with test functions is the stationary-sheet source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) with tangential current $K=0$ and $S=\partial D$; and the field pair $(E,0)$ together with the source pair $(\rho_v+\sigma\,\delta_{\partial D},\ 0)$ satisfies the adopted distributional vacuum Maxwell equations [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]]. Inside the conductor the field vanishes: $E\equiv0$ on $D$ (the **equilibrium condition**); equivalently the conductor interior is field-free and carries no volume charge.
(c) [Potential and equipotential convention] there is a function $\varphi\in C^0(\Omega)\cap C^2(\Omega_v)$ with $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\Omega_v$ and with $\varphi$ constant on each conductor body, $\varphi|_{D_j}\equiv V_j$ for real constants $V_j$ (volts, [[def-em-si-conventions]]); by continuity of $\varphi$ the trace of $\varphi$ on each $\partial D_j$ from the vacuum side equals $V_j$ as well. This is the single-function convention of an ideal conductor with no double layer: the model reads the same potential value on both sides of $\partial D$, while the normal component of $E$ may jump.
(d) [Data] a model is completed either by the component potentials $V_1,\dots,V_m$ together with the volume source $\rho_v$ and the data on $\partial\Omega$ where the laboratory region is bounded, or by the component total charges $Q_j:=\int_{\partial D_j}\sigma\,dS$ (C) together with those same ambient data. These are two declared data types; the postulate asserts neither that both data types are simultaneously specifiable nor that either is solvable for arbitrary data.
(e) [Scope] This is a static, frame-relative equilibrium idealization: it excludes transient finite-conductivity dynamics, relaxation to equilibrium, moving surface charge, electrode polarization and contact effects, and it is not derived from a microscopic matter model. It asserts no existence or uniqueness theorem (those are separate conditional results), no force, no energy, no radiation, no measurement and no apparatus realization; the value $V_j$ is a model parameter and the surface density $\sigma$ is an idealization variable determined by the equilibrium problem when it is solvable.
before.strategy: Nonproof formulation and scope review: adopt the equilibrium objects already defined in the framework and record their exact interfaces instead of proving a physical law. Textbook conductor treatments support each clause as a model choice: the vanishing interior field with all charge on the surface and the constant potential of an equipotential conductor ([[def-em-weak-sources]]'s stationary-sheet source is the framework's own surface-distribution object), the grounded/fixed-potential and fixed-charge data distinction, and the idealization's limits are stated rather than hidden. The mathematical identities used to name the objects are exact: $\partial D$ is a finite disjoint union of compact embedded smooth hypersurfaces and $\Omega_v$ is a bounded smooth domain by [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]] and [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]]; the surface pairing $\sigma\delta_{\partial D}$ is the one of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) under the surface-distribution conventions of [[def-em-surface-distribution]] and carries its declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the field, source and regime objects are those of [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]]; and the adopted solution predicate is [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], not a consequence of the smooth postulate. after.statement:

No experiment is reported and no empirical value is inferred; this is an explicitly adopted equilibrium idealization together with its geometric and source conventions.
(a) [Geometry] a laboratory region $\Omega\times I$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ an arbitrary open ambient region, a finite family $D_1,\dots,D_m$ ($m\ge1$) of bounded $C^\infty$ domains with pairwise disjoint closures in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] with closures strictly inside $\Omega$ (the **conductor bodies**), the **conductor** $D:=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_m$, its **surface** $\partial D$, and the **vacuum region** $\Omega_v:=\Omega\setminus\overline D$. By [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]], $\partial D=\partial D_1\cup\cdots\cup\partial D_m$ is a disjoint union of compact embedded $C^\infty$ hypersurfaces. $$-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0\quad\text{on }\Omega_v,\qquad \varphi|_{\partial\Omega_v}=g,$$
with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]];

$$\int_{\Omega_v^{(j)}}\rho\,dx+\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial\Omega_v^{(j)}}g\,dS=0\qquad\text{for every connected component }\Omega_v^{(j)}\text{ of }\Omega_v,$$

after.title: Declared classical/weak boundary existence theorem
after.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the cited solvability theorem ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega_v\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] with finitely many connected components (the vacuum region of the additional bounded $C^\infty$ ambient branch of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] by [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]], or any bounded smooth domain), let $\rho$ be smooth on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ (fixed-time volume source density, C m$^{-3}$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]]) and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be the framework constant. Then the electrostatic boundary value problems on $\Omega_v$ are solvable in the following exact senses, and the solutions are the fields of the pure electrostatic regime [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with volume source $\rho$:
(a) [Dirichlet branch] for every $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$ there is exactly one $\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ with
$$-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0\quad\text{on }\Omega_v,\qquad \varphi|_{\partial\Omega_v}=g,$$
with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]];
and it is the unique weak $H^1$ solution with trace $g$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] for the class); the field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ ([[def-em-fields]]) is $C^\infty$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ and $(E,0)$ realises the pure electrostatic regime with source $\rho$ on the vacuum region.
(b) [Neumann branch] for every $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$ with
$$\int_{\Omega_v^{(j)}}\rho\,dx+\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial\Omega_v^{(j)}}g\,dS=0\qquad\text{for every connected component }\Omega_v^{(j)}\text{ of }\Omega_v,$$
there is $\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ with $-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $\partial_\nu\varphi=g$ (outward normal $\nu$, [[def-classical-normal-derivative]]), unique up to one additive constant per connected component; the normalisation $\int_{\Omega_v^{(j)}}\varphi\,dx=0$ for every $j$ selects exactly one. The compatibility is also necessary in the sense of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](b).
(c) [Conductor reading and surface-charge realization] for the separated compact-body conductor geometry and zero-interior-volume convention of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], additionally assuming $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ ambient domain, with outer boundary data $g_0\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ on $\partial\Omega$ and constants $V_j$ on the conductor surfaces $\partial D_j$ (constant functions are smooth on the compact disjoint boundary pieces), the combined datum is a special case of (a); the field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\Omega_v$ extended by $E:=0$ on the conductor satisfies the adopted distributional vacuum Maxwell equations [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]] with the source pair $(\rho_v+\sigma\,\delta_{\partial D},\,0)$, where $\sigma:=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+\in C^\infty(\partial D)$ is the constructed continuous surface-charge density, agreeing afterwards with [[pthm-em-conductor-surface-charge]] ([[def-em-weak-sources]](c), [[def-em-surface-distribution]], [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]]); the total charges $Q_j=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}n\cdot E_+\,dS$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]) are thereby determined by the data, and $\varphi$ is constant on each $\partial D_j$ with value $V_j$.
(d) [Stationary sheet charge in the vacuum region] for finitely many disjoint closed smooth interfaces $\Gamma$ strictly inside $\Omega_v$, a smooth sheet density $\sigma_\Gamma$ on them, and outer Dirichlet data $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$, there is a weak solution $\varphi\in H^1(\Omega_v)$ which is $C^\infty$ on the closure of each side of every $\Gamma$, unique by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](c)(iii), solving the weak equation with right-hand side $\int_{\Omega_v}\rho v+\sum_\Gamma\int_\Gamma\sigma_\Gamma\,Tv$; its flux jump is $n\cdot[\varepsilon_0\nabla\varphi]=-\sigma_\Gamma$, equivalently $n\cdot[E]=\sigma_\Gamma/\varepsilon_0$ in the sign convention of [[pthm-em-fixed-vacuum-jumps]]. This is the vacuum ($\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0$) transmission branch; no dielectric coefficient is introduced.
(e) [Scope] all existence statements are the ones proved in [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]] for its stated smooth bounded domains, smooth uniformly positive coefficients (here $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0 I$), smooth data and finitely many disjoint smooth interfaces; the coefficient is the smooth positive constant $\varepsilon_0I$ on every side in the transmission clause. Excluded: nonsmooth boundaries, corners, edges, coefficient loss of regularity, prescribed total charges for conductor bodies (the free equipotential problem), unbounded exterior regions without a stated decay class, dielectric material response (belonging to the material-response page) and any measurement, apparatus or empirical claim. The theorem asserts existence of the potential, not of a physical equilibrium; the ideal conductor is the adopted model of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]].

before.title: Image candidate solves a specified grounded-plane problem
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) inherited from the Newtonian, polar and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$$H:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_3>0\},\qquad \Pi:=\{x_3=0\},\qquad p:=a e_3\ (a>0),$$
let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a charge parameter (coulombs) and $\varepsilon_0>0$ the framework constant ([[def-em-si-conventions]]). Define, with arbitrary values on the exceptional sets,
$$\varphi_I(x):=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac1{|x-p|}-\frac1{|x+ae_3|}\right)\quad(x\in H\setminus\{p\}),\qquad E_I:=-\nabla\varphi_I.$$ The map $E_I$ is a spatial field of [[def-em-fields]] in the fixed-time reading, with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Then:
(a) [Candidate field] $\varphi_I\in C^\infty(H\setminus\{p\})$ and $\Delta\varphi_I=0$ pointwise on $H\setminus\{p\}$: the first term is the Coulomb potential of $p$, whose $n=3$ fundamental solution is harmonic off its pole ([[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]], [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d)), and the second term is $C^\infty$ and harmonic on the whole of $H$ because its pole $-ae_3$ lies outside $H$; $E_I$ is $C^\infty$ on $H\setminus\{p\}$.
(b) [Distributional point source] $\varphi_I\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(H)$ and
$$-\Delta T_{\varphi_I}=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\,\delta_p\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(H),$$
where $T_{\varphi_I}$ is the regular distribution of $\varphi_I$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\delta_p$ the Dirac distribution at $p$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); moreover the field satisfies $\operatorname{div}E_I=(q/\varepsilon_0)\delta_p$ and $\operatorname{curl}E_I=0$ in $\mathcal D'(H)$, where the divergence and curl of $E_I$ are the distributional derivatives of its components ([[def-distributional-derivative]]). Thus $(E_I,0)$ is a pure electrostatic model on $H$ with the fixed-time point source $q\delta_p$, the static reading of the stationary point charge of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)).
(c) [Boundary trace and decay] $\varphi_I$ extends continuously to $\overline H\setminus\{p\}$ with $\varphi_I=0$ on $\Pi$ (the two denominators are equal there), and for $|x|\ge2a$ the cancellation bound holds:
$$|\varphi_I(x)|\le\frac{2|q|\,a}{\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2}.$$
The bound follows by applying the mean value theorem along the segment from $-ae_3$ to $ae_3$ to the function $y\mapsto|x-y|^{-1}$, whose gradient is bounded by $(|x|-a)^{-2}$ there ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). In particular $\varphi_I(x)\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in $H$.
(d) [Uniqueness in the declared class] let $\psi:H\setminus\{p\}\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and harmonic on $H\setminus\{p\}$, continuous on $\overline H\setminus\{p\}$, with $\psi=0$ on $\Pi$, $\psi(x)-\varphi_I(x)\to0$ as $x\to p$ and $\psi(x)\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in $H$. Then $\psi=\varphi_I$ on $H\setminus\{p\}$. Equivalently, the Dirichlet problem $\Delta\psi=0$ on $H\setminus\{p\}$, $\psi=0$ on $\Pi$, with the leading singularity of the point charge at $p$ and decay at infinity, has exactly one solution in the stated class.
(e) [Physics reading: ideal grounded plane in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]] the ideal grounded conducting half-space $\{x_3<0\}$ with the field $E_I$ on $H$, $E\equiv0$ below $\Pi$ and the induced density $\sigma:=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+|_\Pi=-\varepsilon_0\,\partial_3\varphi_I|_\Pi$ (using the normal $n=e_3$ from the conductor into the vacuum; $\sigma\in C^\infty(\Pi\setminus\{0\})$) is a model of the same equilibrium structure as [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]]: it is a pure electrostatic field on $H$ with the point source at $p$ and the equipotential boundary condition $\varphi_I=0$ on $\Pi$; the pair $(E_I,0)$ satisfies the static electrostatic equations with source $q\delta_p$ on $H$, and the induced density is normalised so that the plane carries the compensating charge. However, the half-space conductor is not a compact conductor body: the plane is not a compact embedded hypersurface, $\Pi$ and $\{x_3<0\}$ are not among the geometric objects of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], the density $\sigma$ is not a declared stationary-sheet source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c), and $\sigma$ is not claimed to satisfy a distributional Maxwell identity in the declared source class. The clause is the explicitly declared idealization whose exact mathematical content is (a)-(d).
(f) [Scope] the statement concerns the ideal point charge above an ideal grounded plane in the declared decay class; it excludes finite-plane edge effects, conductor thickness, transients, moving charges, radiation, self-force and any measurement; no uniqueness is asserted outside the class of (d), and the point-source singularity is never evaluated.
before.strategy:
(a) $|x-p|^{-1}$ is the $n=3$ fundamental solution kernel, harmonic off its pole, and $|x+ae_3|^{-1}$ is $C^\infty$ on $H$ because $|x+ae_3|\ge a>0$ there; sums of harmonic functions are harmonic by linearity of second derivatives ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and $
abla\varphi_I$ is computed off the pole by the chain and power rules ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). (b) Local integrability: $|x-p|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in dimension three and $|x+ae_3|^{-1}$ is continuous, so both have locally integrable components and the sum does (measurability is [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]) ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); the identification with regular distributions is [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. The distributional Laplacian of the first term is $(q/\varepsilon_0)\delta_p$ on $\mathbb R^3$ and hence on the open subset $H$ ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d), [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]), while the second term $u(x):=-(q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0))|x+ae_3|^{-1}$ is $C^\infty$ on $H$ with $\Delta u=0$ classically; for every compactly supported test $\eta\in\mathcal D(H)$ and every coordinate interval containing its support, [[thm-integration-by-parts]] gives $\langle\partial_iT_u,\etaangle=-\int u\,\partial_i\eta=\int(\partial_iu)\eta$, so $\partial_iT_u=T_{\partial_iu}$; applying the same identity to the $C^\infty$ function $\partial_iu$ gives $\partial_i\partial_iT_u=T_{\partial_i\partial_iu}$, and summing gives $\Delta T_u=T_{\Delta u}=0$ as the regular distribution of the zero function ([[def-distribution]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). Adding the two contributions proves the displayed identity, and $\operatorname{div}E_I=-\Delta T_{\varphi_I}$, $\operatorname{curl}E_I=0$ follow because $E_I=-
abla\varphi_I$ off the pole and the mixed second derivatives of a regular distribution commute ([[def-distributional-derivative]]). The reading of $q\delta_p$ as the fixed-time point source is the dictionary of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e) and [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) on the half-space; the pair $(E_I,0)$ is then a pure electrostatic model there. (c) On $\Pi$ the two distances $|x-p|$ and $|x+ae_3|$ are equal, so the bracket vanishes; continuity on $\overline H\setminus\{p\}$ is continuity of the two kernels away from their poles. For the bound, write $f(y):=|x-y|^{-1}$ and apply the mean value theorem to $f$ on the segment from $-ae_3$ to $ae_3$: $|f(ae_3)-f(-ae_3)|\le 2a\sup_{|y|\le a}|
abla f(y)|$ with $|
abla f(y)|=|x-y|^{-2}\le(|x|-a)^{-2}$ ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]); for $|x|\ge2a$ this is at most $4|x|^{-2}$, giving the displayed constant after multiplication by $|q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$. (d) Apply [[lem-em-half-space-harmonic-uniqueness-with-decay]] to $w=\psi-\varphi_I$: both terms are $C^2$ harmonic on $H\setminus\{p\}$ and continuous on $\overline H\setminus\{p\}$, the trace on $\Pi$ vanishes because both do, and both limits at $p$ cancel and at infinity vanish by the bound of (c) and the hypothesis on $\psi$. The lemma yields $w=0$. (e)-(f) record the reading and scope: the geometric and source-theoretic exclusions are exactly those of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] and [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) (noncompact plane), and no identity beyond (a)-(d) is claimed. The choice cost is the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the cited integral and distribution interfaces.

$$\varphi_j|_{\partial D_k}=\delta_{jk},\qquad \varphi_j|_{\partial\Omega}=0,$$

$$C_{jk}:=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\frac{\partial\varphi_k}{\partial\nu}\,dS,\qquad j,k=1,\dots,m,$$
the flux integrals of continuous functions over the compact embedded hypersurfaces $\partial D_j$ (normal derivative of [[def-classical-normal-derivative]]) ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]]). Then:
(a) [Linearity and matrix form] for every $V=(V_1,\dots,V_m)\in\mathbb R^m$ the unique equilibrium potential with conductor potentials $V$ and grounded outer boundary is $\varphi^V=\sum_{j=1}^mV_j\varphi_j$, and the conductor charges of [[pthm-em-conductor-surface-charge]](d) are
$$Q_j(V)=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\frac{\partial\varphi^V}{\partial\nu}\,dS=\sum_{k=1}^mC_{jk}V_k,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad Q=CV.$$
(b) [Reciprocity] $C$ is symmetric: $C_{jk}=C_{kj}$ for all $j,k$; the symmetry is Green's symmetric pairing of the harmonic potentials $\varphi_j,\varphi_k$.
(c) [Energy identity] the field energy of the configuration is
$$U(V)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\Omega_v}|\nabla\varphi^V|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac12V^{T}CV=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^mV_jQ_j(V),$$

(d) [Two-conductor reading] with only conductor $1$ driven and every other conductor grounded, $V=te_1$: $Q_1=C_{11}t$, $Q_j=C_{j1}t$ for $j\ne1$, and $U=\tfrac12C_{11}t^2=\tfrac12Q_1V_1=Q_1^2/(2C_{11})$; the **capacitance of the arrangement** at conductor $1$ with respect to the grounded reference is the positive geometric number $C_{11}=Q_1/V_1>0$, and the energy identities $U=\tfrac12QV=Q^2/(2C)=\tfrac12CV^2$ hold with $C=C_{11}$, $Q=Q_1$, $V=V_1$. u\varphi_k-\varphi_k\partial_
u\varphi_j igr)dS;$$

before.title: External force from mirror field with self-field excluded
before.statement:
In the ideal grounded-plane configuration of [[pthm-em-image-method-certificate]]: vacuum half-space $H=\{x_3>0\}$, point charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ at $p=ae_3$ ($a>0$), field $E_I$ given by the image potential, and $E_I$ has the Coulomb singularity $(q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0))(x-p)/|x-p|^3$ of the source charge as $x\to p$ ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d), [[def-em-fields]]). Split the field near $p$ as
$$E_I(x)=E_q(x)+E_{\rm ext}(x),\qquad E_q(x):=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{x-p}{|x-p|^3}\quad(x\ne p),$$
the **self-field** $E_q$ of the source charge and the **external (mirror) field** $E_{\rm ext}:=E_I-E_q$, which is $C^\infty$ on a neighbourhood of $p$ (it is minus the gradient of the smooth mirror term $-q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)|x+ae_3|^{-1}$). Then:
(a) [External field at the charge] the external field at the location of the charge is
$$E_{\rm ext}(p)=-\frac{q}{16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}\,e_3 .$$
It is the gradient of the mirror term evaluated at $p$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).
(b) [Force on the held charge] under the adopted external Lorentz coupling [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](i) at zero velocity, a test particle of charge $q$ held at $p$ experiences the electric force
$$F=q\,E_{\rm ext}(p)=-\frac{q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}\,e_3,$$
attractive toward the plane, of magnitude $q^2/(16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2)$; the particle's own field is excluded from the coupling by the postulate, so the result is a two-body-style external force of the mirror field and is not a self-force.
(c) [Reading and scope] for either sign of $q$ the force is attractive (the magnitude depends on $q^2$); the induced total plane charge is $-q$ and its distribution is concentrated under the charge; the example is the exact ideal-model result for a held point charge, an ideal grounded plane and the adopted static external force law. It asserts no measurement, no dynamics of the charge (no motion or radiation), no finite-plane or finite-conductor correction, no self-force and no claim that the pair of idealisations is realised by an apparatus; the source is the idealised stationary point charge of [[pthm-em-image-method-certificate]](e), not a declared compact-source model.

Both $E_I$ and $E_q$ are gradients off $p$; subtracting, $E_{m ext}=-
abla u$ with $u(x):=-\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{1}{|x+ae_3|}$, which is $C^\infty$ on the ball $|x-p|<a$ because $|x+ae_3|\ge a>0$ there ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). Differentiating $u$ by the chain and power rules gives $
abla u(x)=+\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{x+ae_3}{|x+ae_3|^3}$ for $x$ in that ball; at $x=p=ae_3$ this is $\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2ae_3}{(2a)^3}=\dfrac{q\,e_3}{16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}$, and $E_{m ext}(p)=-
abla u(p)=-\dfrac{q}{16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}e_3$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). This proves (a). For (b): [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](i) adopts the covariant equation of motion with the prescribed external field and explicitly excludes the particle's own field; at zero coordinate velocity the magnetic term vanishes and the coordinate force is $q$ times the external electric field, so the displayed force follows by substituting (a) ([[def-em-si-conventions]] fixes the units, N). The magnitude and attraction statements are immediate from the formula and $q^2\ge0$ with equality only for $q=0$, in which case there is no charge and no force. Clause (c) records the idealization: the total induced charge $-q$ is the induced-charge normalisation of the ideal plane recorded with the certificate, and nothing dynamical, radiative, measured or finite-geometry is claimed.

before.title: Large plate capacitor with fringing approximation
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the integral and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). **Declare the ideal parallel-plate model** of two infinite parallel charged planes in vacuo, read as equipotential ideal conductor surfaces of the same equilibrium structure as [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] (the pure electrostatic regime [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with fields [[def-em-fields]]): for a separation parameter $d>0$, half-separation $h=d/2$, a surface-density parameter $\sigma>0$ (C m$^{-2}$) and the framework constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], the model consists of the field
$$E(x):=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}e_3,&|x_3|<h,\\[2pt]0,&|x_3|>h,\end{cases}\qquad x=(x_1,x_2,x_3),$$
together with the plane densities $+\sigma$ on $\Pi_+:=\{x_3=h\}$ and $-\sigma$ on $\Pi_-:=\{x_3=-h\}$, and with the piecewise potential $\varphi(x):=-\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}x_3$ for $|x_3|\le h$, $\varphi:=-\dfrac{\sigma h}{\varepsilon_0}$ for $x_3\ge h$ and $\varphi:=+\dfrac{\sigma h}{\varepsilon_0}$ for $x_3\le-h$. Then:
(a) [Direct distributional verification] $E$ and $\varphi$ are locally integrable and $C^\infty$ off $\Pi_+\cup\Pi_-$ with $E=-\nabla\varphi$ there, $\varphi$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3$ and constant on each plane with the values $\varphi|_{\Pi_+}=-\sigma h/\varepsilon_0$, $\varphi|_{\Pi_-}=+\sigma h/\varepsilon_0$; and in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$
$$\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\bigl(\delta_{\Pi_+}-\delta_{\Pi_-}\bigr),\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,$$
where $\delta_{\Pi_\pm}(\psi):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\psi(x_1,x_2,\pm h)\,dx_1\,dx_2$ for compactly supported smooth $\psi$ are the plane distributions defined by the iterated Lebesgue integrals. Equivalently, the model realises the static electrostatic equations with the declared pair of plane densities and no other source, and the potential differences read off $\varphi$ are $\varphi(-h)-\varphi(h)=2\sigma h/\varepsilon_0=\sigma d/\varepsilon_0$.
(b) [Uniform field and voltage] the field between the planes has constant magnitude $|E|=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ and is normal to the planes, and the potential difference between the plates is $V:=\varphi|_{\Pi_-}-\varphi|_{\Pi_+}=\sigma d/\varepsilon_0$.
(c) [Charge, capacitance and energy of the ideal model] for any chosen finite area $A>0$ the charge on the portion of area $A$ of the positive plate is $Q:=\sigma A$, so $Q=(\varepsilon_0A/d)V$ with the geometric ratio
$$C:=\frac QV=\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}>0,$$
independent of $\sigma$ and $V$; and the field energy contained in the slab of area $A$ between the plates is
$$U=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\text{slab of area }A}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac{\sigma^2Ad}{2\varepsilon_0}=\frac12QV=\frac{Q^2}{2C}=\frac12CV^2 .$$
(d) [Relation to the bounded-conductor theorem and scope] the linearity $Q=CV$, the positivity $C>0$ and the energy identities $U=\frac12QV=\frac{Q^2}{2C}=\frac12CV^2$ are exactly the conclusions that [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]] proves for bounded conductor configurations with prescribed potentials and a grounded reference; this example verifies them directly for the ideal model because the infinite planes and the unbounded declared field are outside that theorem's hypotheses (compact conductors in a bounded vacuum region) and outside the declared stationary-sheet source type of [[def-em-weak-sources]], exactly as the ideal line source lies outside the compact-source types of the electrostatic page. No approximation theorem from finite plates to the infinite model is asserted; for a finite real plate pair the uniform-field model neglects the fringing field near the edges, which is not computed here, and the idealisation also omits the finite-thickness, material, transient and measurement content of any real capacitor.
before.strategy: All identities are computed directly from the explicit piecewise formulas; no compact-sheet jump theorem is invoked, because the planes are noncompact and the model is a declared idealization. (a) Local integrability is immediate from the boundedness of the piecewise field and the finiteness of the slab's intersections with compact sets ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]); the identification with regular distributions is [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. For a compactly supported smooth test $\psi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]), $\langle\operatorname{div}E,\psi\rangle=-\int E\cdot\nabla\psi=-\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{|x_3|<h}\partial_3\psi\,d\lambda_3$ (inner product [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and norm of [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]); Fubini ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) writes the slab integral as $\int_{\mathbb R^2}\bigl(\int_{-h}^{h}\partial_3\psi(x_1,x_2,s)\,ds\bigr)dx_1dx_2$, and the inner integral is $\psi(x_1,x_2,h)-\psi(x_1,x_2,-h)$ by [[thm-integration-by-parts]] (the one-dimensional Newton-Leibniz identity, applicable because $\psi$ is smooth and compactly supported and the interval is bounded); hence $\langle\operatorname{div}E,\psi\rangle=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}(\delta_{\Pi_+}-\delta_{\Pi_-})(\psi)$, proving the divergence identity with the sign convention of [[def-distributional-derivative]] and [[def-distribution]]. The curl identity: $E_1=E_2=0$ and $E_3=-\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\mathbf 1_{\{|x_3|<h\}}$ is a function of $x_3$ alone, so its distributional $x_1$- and $x_2$-derivatives vanish identically ([[def-distributional-derivative]]); hence $\operatorname{curl}E=(\partial_2E_3-\partial_3E_2,\partial_3E_1-\partial_1E_3,\partial_1E_2-\partial_2E_1)=0$. The potential formulas give $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on the three open regions ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and continuity across the planes is the equality of the two one-sided constants. before.title: Incompatible total flux forbids a solution
before.statement:
Let $B:=B_1(0)=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|<1\}$ be the open unit ball, a bounded $C^\infty$ (in particular $C^1$) domain with $\partial B=S^2$ and outward normal $\nu(x)=x$ ([[lem-em-euclidean-balls-and-annuli-are-bounded-c-one-domains]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and consider the pure electrostatic Neumann problem on $B$ (regime [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], fields [[def-em-fields]], constants [[def-em-si-conventions]]) with **zero volume source and unit normal field**:
$$-\Delta\varphi=0\ \text{ in }B,\qquad \partial_\nu\varphi=1\ \text{ on }\partial B .$$
Then:
(a) [No classical solution] there is no real $\varphi\in C^2(\overline B)$ satisfying these equations: if such a $\varphi$ existed, [[lem-neumann-compatibility-from-the-divergence-theorem]] with $f=-\Delta\varphi=0$ and $g=\partial_\nu\varphi\equiv1$ would give
$$0=\int_B f\,d\lambda_3=-\int_{\partial B}g\,dS=-|S^2|=-4\pi,$$
because the surface area of the unit sphere is $|S^2|=4\pi$ ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]); the contradiction is the failure of the necessary flux compatibility of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](b).
(b) [No weak solution] more generally there is no $u\in H^1(B)$ with $\int_B\nabla v\cdot\nabla u\,d\lambda_3=\langle g,Tv\rangle$ for all $v\in H^1(B)$ with $g\equiv1$ read as an element of the dual trace space ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]): testing $v\equiv1$ would force $\ell(1)=\int_{\partial B}1\,dS=4\pi=0$, and the weak Neumann existence lemma states existence exactly when $\ell(1)=0$ ([[lem-em-weak-neumann-and-transmission-existence]]); equivalently the unit ball's boundary flux budget fails already in the weak formulation.
(c) [Physics reading and scope] in the pure electrostatic regime the datum $\partial_\nu\varphi\equiv1$ on the whole boundary of the unit ball is inadmissible: no electrostatic potential with zero volume source satisfies it, and the obstruction is the strictly positive total boundary flux $4\pi$, not a smoothness or compactness artefact. The admissible Neumann data are exactly those satisfying the necessary compatibility $\int_{\partial B}g\,dS=0$ for the zero-source problem, which is a flux budget and not an existence theorem (sufficiency at the smooth level is the separate content of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-existence]](b) under its hypotheses). The item is a mathematical impossibility statement about the ideal boundary value problem: it reports no measurement, no apparatus and no material property, and the companion failure with unit source and zero boundary field is the same flux obstruction, obtained by evaluating that lemma with $f\equiv1$ and $g\equiv0$.

before.title: Poincare inequality with mean subtraction on a bounded connected C-one domain
before.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice (used through the smooth-up-to-the-boundary density theorem below) and the Axiom of Countable Choice (declared by the flattening and Sobolev suppliers). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain in the graph sense ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], [[def-connected-space]]); its closure is compact, so the boundary has a finite cover by boundary charts ([[def-compact-space]]). There is a constant $C_\Omega$, depending only on $\Omega$, with $$\|v-v_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\,\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1(\Omega),\qquad v_\Omega:=\frac1{|\Omega|}\int_\Omega v\,dx .$$ Here $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with the weak coordinate derivatives, and $\nabla v$ denotes the weak gradient. The estimate is the mean-zero (Poincare) inequality needed for weak Neumann solvability, where the mean-zero subspace carries the gradient norm.
before.strategy:
On a rectangular box $R$ the one-dimensional fundamental theorem along coordinate segments with Cauchy-Schwarz ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) gives $\int_R\int_R|v(x)-v(y)|^2dx\,dy\le C_R|R|\int_R|
abla v|^2dx$; replacing $x$ by $y$ one coordinate at a time bounds the squared finite sum by three times the sum of the three one-coordinate differences, and Fubini-Tonelli ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) integrates the remaining coordinates. before.title: Weak Neumann and transmission existence with interface charges
before.statement:
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain, let $\varepsilon$ be measurable symmetric uniformly elliptic, let $ho\in L^2(\Omega)$, and let $g\in H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$, the bounded real dual of the boundary trace space ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]). Define $\ell(v)=\int_\Omegaho v+\langle g,Tvangle$ on $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]). A weak Neumann solution is a $u\in H^1$ with $$\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla u=\ell(v)\qquad	ext{for every }v\in H^1(\Omega).$$ Such a solution exists if and only if $\ell(1)=0$, and is then unique up to an additive constant; normalising $\int_\Omega u=0$ makes it unique. On finitely many connected components the compatibility and normalisation are imposed separately on each component. For finitely many disjoint smooth stationary interfaces with piecewise smooth uniformly elliptic $\varepsilon$, bulk data $ho\in L^2$ and prescribed sheet charge $\sigma$ on the interfaces defining a bounded trace functional on $H^1$ (for instance $\sigma\in L^2$ of each smooth compact interface), the same argument gives weak Dirichlet or compatible Neumann existence for the transmission problem, with the globally $H^1$ potential having identical one-sided trace; where the solution is classically smooth on each side, integration by parts gives the jump $n\cdot[\varepsilon
abla u]=-\sigma$, equivalently $n\cdot[D]=\sigma$. General piecewise classical regularity remains a separate requirement.
before.strategy: The trace bound of the prescribed-data lemma and Holder's inequality make $|\ell(v)|\le C\|v\|_{H^1}$ ([[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]], [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]). Testing the equation with $v=1$ makes $\ell(1)=0$ necessary. The mean-zero subspace of $H^1$ is closed, and the mean-zero coercivity lemma makes its gradient norm equivalent to the complete $H^1$ norm ([[lem-em-mean-zero-coercivity-on-a-c-one-domain]]); the symmetric coercive variational solver ([[lem-em-symmetric-coercive-variational-solver]]) solves the coercive symmetric form there. Every $v\in H^1$ is its mean-zero part plus a constant, and the constant term contributes zero on both sides by compatibility, so this solves the full problem; for the difference of two solutions tested against itself the gradient vanishes, and the mean-zero inequality makes the difference constant. Each finite disjoint component is treated separately. The transmission case replaces $\ell$ by the sum of the bulk, boundary and interface trace functionals of the prescribed sheet charge; the same variational argument applies, and the one-sided trace identity holds for the globally $H^1$ potential by trace continuity in each chart, giving the stated jump relation where the solution is classically smooth on each side.

before.title: Classical elliptic regularity on smooth domains and across smooth interfaces
before.statement: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain, let $\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}^3)$ be uniformly positive, and let $\rho$ be smooth on the closure. Prescribe in the prescribed-data lemma either smooth Dirichlet data $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega)$, or smooth outward flux data $g$ with its compatibility condition as in the weak Neumann lemma. Then the weak solution of $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon\nabla u)=\rho$ in $\Omega$ with those data is $C^\infty$ on the closure $\overline\Omega$. For finitely many disjoint closed smooth interfaces strictly inside $\Omega$, piecewise smooth positive $\varepsilon$, piecewise smooth $\rho$ and smooth sheet charge $\sigma$, the weak solution is smooth on each closed side. Edge and junction points, reentrant corners and coefficient loss of regularity are excluded. The existence claims are those of the two weak solvability lemmas; this lemma proves their classical upgrade on the declared domains.
before.strategy:
Local estimate. In an interior patch, or in a flattened smooth boundary/interface patch, write the weak equation in divergence form $\int a_{ij}\partial_ju\,\partial_iv=\int fv+\int G_i\partial_iv$ with the transformed coefficients $	ilde a=|\det D\Phi^{-1}|\,D\Phi\,a\,D\Phi^{\mathsf T}$; positivity of the Jacobian bounds and the bounds on $D\Phi$ preserve uniform ellipticity. Dirichlet data are removed by subtracting the smooth lift $g(y)\eta(t)$ built from a finite subordinate smooth partition and a normal cutoff; smooth Neumann flux is converted to smooth volume data by a collar vector field $G$ with $G\cdot n=g$ and the divergence theorem. For a tangential difference quotient $\delta_h^ku$ with a cutoff $\eta$ supported in a smaller patch, test the weak identity with $v=-\delta_{-h}^k(\eta^2w)$; change of variables and the product identity give the principal bound $\alpha\|\eta
abla w\|_2^2$ against cutoff terms $C\|u\|_{H^1}[\|\eta
abla w\|_2+\|w\|_2]$, the crucial increment estimates $\|\delta_hu\|_{L^2}\le\|\partial_ku\|_{L^2}$ (from the ACL line identity and Jensen) and $\|\delta_ha\|_\infty\le\|\partial_ka\|_\infty$, and $f,G$ terms; Cauchy-Schwarz and $2AB\le(\alpha/2)A^2+2B^2/\alpha$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) absorb the gradient terms, giving uniform difference-quotient bounds. With compactly supported tests the weak identity is $-\operatorname{div}(a
abla u)=f-\operatorname{div}G$ distributionally. Expanding that divergence, at a boundary or interface the normal second derivative is recovered from $a_{33}\partial_{33}u=\operatorname{div}G-f-\sum_{(i,j)
e(3,3)}a_{ij}\partial_{ij}u-\sum_{ij}(\partial_ia_{ij})\partial_ju$ with $a_{33}\ge\alpha>0$. A finite cover of the compact closure gives global $H^2$ bounds on each declared side. Derivatives agree with the weak ones by testing and Fubini, representatives agree by continuity, and arbitrarily large $m$ gives a $C^\infty$ representative on the closure whose continuous trace is the prescribed one.
